archetypes.name: EU retail bank under DORA
archetypes.summary: Mid-size retail and SME bank headquartered in the EU (Germany and the Netherlands), 4,000 staff, Azure plus own data centres, Microsoft 365 and a US AI API; uses AI for credit decisions.

Customer of cloud services in the EU: switching rights, charges abolished from 12 Jan 2027

exposure.why: TIA partial, sub-processor control partial, data map partial; nothing absent
Register of information and exit plans partial; concentration assessed but high
AI Act role and risk mapping partial

Data-flow map and records of processing partial or out of date (GDPR Art. 30)
DORA Art. 28(8) exit plans for some services only; the Art. 28(3) register of information (also partial) ranks sixth

archetypes.reasoning: DORA applies to EU credit institutions from 17 Jan 2025 (Art. 2(1); validation rows 16, 20) [S7]. GDPR applies through the EU establishment (Art. 3(1)) [S8]. Credit scoring is an Annex III 5(b) use (validation row 8), so the bank is a deployer of a high-risk system with duties from 2 Dec 2027 under Regulation (EU) 2026/1744 [S12]; the AI Act cap is quantified because a high-risk duty applies (H4). NIS2 is advisory, not `applies`: banking is an Annex I sector, but the bank is a DORA financial entity and has assessed itself out of NIS2 scope; the DORA-as-sector-specific-act position (NIS2 Art. 4) is UNSOURCED in this session and must be confirmed in S2. No legal level floor applies (3.3): the L2/L3 requirement is the board's choice, which is typical for EU banks but is not a DORA requirement. The headline gaps are therefore key custody and provider access (L2 controls), then sub-processor control (required by both GDPR Art. 28 and the DORA subcontracting RTS), the data map and DORA exit plans (Art. 28(8)); the DORA register of information (Art. 28(3)) is also partial and ranks sixth under the tie-break rule in 8.3 (validation rows 21, 23, 85). Executive mode is lower (50) than workshop (55) because, with one L2 level for every class, source code in a US SaaS counts as outside the zone; the workshop sets proprietary data to L1 with the US allowed. Largest cap: GDPR Art. 83(5), 4% of EUR 3.2bn = EUR 128M, above the AI Act Art. 99(4) figure of 3% = EUR 96M; DORA penalties for financial entities are national (Art. 50–51), so they are not quantified. Never summed.

archetypes.reasoning: UK GDPR applies through the UK establishment [S15, S18]. A Solvency II insurer is PRA-regulated, so SS1/21 operational resilience (with FCA PS21/3) and SS2/21 outsourcing apply (validation rows 38–40) [S19, S20]. The UK CTP regime binds the designated providers, not the insurer; it is advisory here because the insurer uses AWS and Azure, whose UK-relevant entities were designated with effect from 13 Jul 2026 (validation rows 42–43) [S21]. EU GDPR, the EU AI Act and the Data Act are not applicable: no EU establishment and no EU data subjects; EU-region backups are processed by EU-established providers, whose own GDPR duties fall on them (a model limit to note for counsel). This archetype shows why there are two headlines: maturity is high (84, Sovereign-ready) because the controls for the chosen L1/L2 levels are largely in place, while the UK GDPR exposure is red because IDTA and Addendum transfers have no transfer risk assessment, which ICO guidance requires for Art. 46 transfers [S16]. Special-category backups in EU regions are lawful under the UK's adequacy regulations for the EEA, so the backup finding is against the board's own UK-only choice, and the finding text says so. UK operational resilience is graded but not RAG-rated: impact tolerances are assessed in Resilience IQ (section 11). Largest cap: 4% of GBP 2.5bn = GBP 100M (above GBP 17.5M), UK GDPR Art. 83(5) and DPA 2018 s.157 (validation row 37).

HIPAA applies because the company is a business associate (45 CFR 160.103) [S28]. CCPA applies: California data subjects and revenue above USD 26,625,000 (CPPA, from 1 Jan 2025) [S27]. NIS2: a SaaS provider is treated as a cloud computing service provider (Annex I, digital infrastructure) because the client chose that sector; at 180 staff it is at least medium-sized, and whether it is large (essential) depends on the balance sheet, which is unknown, so the grade is `applies` with the class to confirm (2.6 `medium_or_large`) [S5, S6]; whether every SaaS is a "cloud computing service" is to be confirmed in S2. The AI Act applies to the company as a provider placing AI features on the EU market (Art. 2(1)(a)) [S12]. The Data Act applies because it provides data processing services to EU customers (Chapter VI) (validation rows 24–27). The DOJ rule is advisory: the company is a US person holding US health data at volume, but no country-of-concern link is reported, so only screening is advised (28 CFR 202.205, 202.601) [S26]. Maturity is Exposed (37): provider-managed keys and unapproved provider access for health data set at L2 are critical gaps, and the transfer-basis control scores 1 because EU routes exist (DPF and SCCs) but no UK route is selected for UK data in the US (the UK Extension needs separate certification; validation row 47). Executive mode reads higher (52) because L1 applies to every class there, so key custody and provider access are not required; the workshop's L2 for health data adds them. Largest cap: GDPR EUR 20M fixed limb, since 4% of USD 75M is lower; the AI Act cap depends on SME status, which is uncertain (balance sheet unknown), so it is shown as a formula.

archetypes.reasoning: EU and UK subsidiaries bring GDPR and UK GDPR in under Art. 3(1) [S8, S15]. The firm assessed itself as an NIS2 important entity, but a managed service provider is an Annex I ICT service management entity and at its size (large) Art. 3(1)(a) points to essential; the rule shows the higher class and asks for confirmation against the national transposition [S5]. The AI Act applies as a provider (Art. 2(1)(a)) [S12]. DORA is advisory: the firm is not a financial entity, but its EU bank clients must flow Art. 30 terms (access, audit, exit assistance) down to it, which is why its weak audit-rights position (reports only) matters commercially [S7]. In India, DPDP applies (Indian employees and processing in India, duties from 13 May 2027; s.17(1)(d) may exempt EU clients' data processed under foreign contracts, status S [S47]) and CERT-In applies (validation row 66). As an SEC registrant it must disclose material incidents within four business days of the materiality determination [S30]. CCPA applies via California data subjects and revenue [S27]; whether employee data is covered is to be confirmed in S2. The critical gap is EU bank clients' financial data processed and backed up in India when the requirement for that class is EEA-only with held keys (L2); location rules are by convention only. Executive mode reads Managed (67) but the workshop reads Developing (45): with one L1 level for all classes, India and the EEA are both allowed zones for every class, and keys and access are not required; the workshop's per-class L2 for EU clients' financial data reveals the gap. This is the reason executive results carry the "requirement set at one level" label (7.1) and open question Q3. Largest cap: GDPR Art. 83(5), 4% of USD 2bn (USD 80M before conversion at the register's dated rate); UK GDPR's 4% is the same percentage and is not added.
